_doc: Reasoning-focused cases. 'p' indexes this case's passages list.
_guideline: SUPPORTED: every part entailed; allowed inference = paraphrase, counting, simple arithmetic, combining passages, version-range containment. CONTRADICTED: if the passages are true the claim must be false (wrong number/version/name for the same thing, negation, reversed comparison, always/never refuted by a stated exception). UNSUPPORTED: neither entailed nor incompatible (extrinsic facts even if true, attribute not stated for that entity, converse of an only-if, added specificity). Modality/quantifier: weakening (always->can, all->some) is SUPPORTED; strengthening (typical->required, can->always) is UNSUPPORTED unless a stated exception refutes it (then CONTRADICTED). Logic: contrapositive is SUPPORTED; converse of an only-if is UNSUPPORTED, or CONTRADICTED when another passage gives a counterexample. Invalid transitive comparisons are UNSUPPORTED.

cases.answer: Because transaction IDs are only 32 bits wide, the XID space holds about 4 billion values, and every normal XID has roughly two billion older and two billion newer XIDs. That is why every table must be vacuumed at least once every two billion transactions; running past that without vacuuming means permanent, unrecoverable data loss. With the default autovacuum_freeze_max_age of 200 million transactions, the anti-wraparound autovacuum kicks in after only about 10% of that two-billion window. The effective maximum for vacuum_freeze_table_age is 95% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age, so with the default it can be at most 180 million. If autovacuum still fails, warnings start when the oldest XIDs are forty million transactions from wraparound and new XIDs are refused once fewer than three million remain, leaving a 37-million-transaction window between the first warning and the hard stop. Once XID assignment stops, no new transactions of any kind can be started.

cases.answer: Autovacuum relies on the statistics collection facility, so if track_counts is off, autovacuum cannot be used; turning track_counts on is by itself enough for autovacuum to work. Even when autovacuum is disabled, PostgreSQL still invokes it on tables that might contain unfrozen rows with XIDs older than autovacuum_freeze_max_age. The launcher tries to start one worker per database every autovacuum_naptime seconds, so with 4 databases and autovacuum_naptime set to 60 seconds, a new worker starts about every 15 seconds. Each database gets at most one worker at a time, and running workers count against max_connections. Autovacuum processes partitions like ordinary tables, but it does not run ANALYZE on partitioned tables, and it does not issue ANALYZE for foreign tables either. Normally a conflicting lock request interrupts autovacuum, and the same is true for an autovacuum that is running to prevent transaction ID wraparound.

cases.answer: Standard VACUUM can run alongside normal SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE traffic, while VACUUM FULL needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table; VACUUM FULL is also the faster of the two because it compacts the table in a single pass. Standard VACUUM never returns space to the operating system. VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and the table-rewriting forms of ALTER TABLE all temporarily need extra disk space roughly equal to the size of the table, so rewriting a 50 GB table needs about another 50 GB free. Since the autovacuum daemon never issues VACUUM FULL, a VACUUM FULL that shows up in your logs was not started by autovacuum. For a table whose entire contents are deleted periodically, TRUNCATE avoids the need for a follow-up VACUUM, at the cost of violating strict MVCC semantics. Installations with extremely high update rates may vacuum their busiest tables as often as every few minutes, and anyone not using autovacuum is required to run a database-wide VACUUM once a day.

cases.answer: Before PostgreSQL 9.4, freezing replaced a row's insertion XID with FrozenTransactionId, so on a cluster still running 9.3 frozen rows show up with an xmin of 2. Newer versions only set a flag bit, mainly to reduce WAL volume, and keep the original xmin, so a cluster that was pg_upgrade'd from 9.3 can never contain rows with xmin 2. System catalogs can also contain rows with xmin 1, BootstrapTransactionId, which is treated as older than every normal XID. pg_xact stores two bits of commit status per transaction, so the default horizon of 200 million transactions costs about 50MB, and raising autovacuum_freeze_max_age to its two-billion maximum would grow pg_xact to roughly 2GB. Multixact member storage can grow to about 20GB before wraparound, and aggressive vacuums start running more often once it passes about half of that. XID exhaustion and MXID exhaustion both block all write transactions.

cases.answer: Because the wal-index lives in shared memory, all processes using a WAL database must be on the same host, so two processes on different machines sharing a database over NFS cannot use WAL. Being on the same host, however, is enough to guarantee that WAL will work. Since there is only one WAL file, two writers can never be writing at the same moment, even though readers can run alongside a writer; this single-writer limit can be lifted with BEGIN CONCURRENT. A process can use WAL without shared memory only if it sets EXCLUSIVE locking mode before its first WAL access, and in that case it stays in EXCLUSIVE mode until it leaves WAL journal mode. With PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, commits skip the WAL sync and the checkpoint is the only operation that issues a sync; with FULL, every commit syncs the WAL. Running the checkpoint in a separate thread therefore guarantees that the main thread never blocks on a sync, whatever the synchronous setting.

cases.answer: If you increment a counter 100 times, the AOF holds 100 entries even though 99 of them are unnecessary, and after a rewrite that key can be rebuilt from a single command. On Redis 2.2 you have to run BGREWRITEAOF yourself, while Redis 2.6 can trigger log rewriting automatically. Redis 2.4 and later never run an AOF rewrite and an RDB snapshot at the same time, and if you request BGREWRITEAOF while a snapshot is running, Redis schedules it and starts it once the snapshot completes. With appendfsync everysec you can lose up to one second of writes, and with appendfsync always no writes are lost in any failure scenario. RDB forks less often than AOF does. When both AOF and RDB are enabled, Redis rebuilds the dataset from the AOF on restart rather than from the RDB file.

cases.answer: A common backup scheme keeps hourly RDB snapshots for the latest 48 hours and daily snapshots for one or two months, which means up to 48 hourly files and as many as about 60 daily files. At least once a day a snapshot should be transferred outside the data center, or at least outside the physical machine. Redis can save the dataset every N seconds if there have been at least M changes, so with a save point of 300 seconds and 100 changes, a crash can never lose more than five minutes of writes. Snapshots sent to S3 should be encrypted, for example with gpg -c, and the password stored in several safe places. If you push backups to a VPS over SCP, verifying the file size after the transfer is enough to guarantee the backup is intact. With appendfsync no, Linux typically flushes data every 30 seconds.

cases.answer: The WAL-reset bug was found on 2026-03-03, and the fixed release, 3.51.3, came out about ten days later. The bug is likely present in releases going back to 3.7.0 from July 2010, so it went unnoticed for more than fifteen years. SQLite 3.51.2, released in January 2026, is likely affected, and the backports to 3.44.6 and 3.50.7 shipped on the same day as 3.51.3. A single-threaded application that only ever opens one connection cannot hit the bug. Because the developers could only trigger it with a special test hook, the bug has never been reproduced without modified SQLite sources. Its observed rate in the wild is no higher than the expected rate of SSD malfunctions, so unless you are doing something really unusual you are unlikely to ever encounter it.

cases.answer: Since Redis 7.0.0 the AOF is split into at most one base file and any number of incremental files, all tracked by a manifest file that is written in JSON. During a rewrite the parent keeps writing to a newly opened incremental file, so if the rewrite fails, the old base and incremental files plus that new incremental file still represent the complete dataset. Failed rewrites are retried at a slower and slower rate. The rewrite produces a new AOF with the minimal set of operations needed to recreate the current dataset. If the AOF is merely truncated at the end, Redis loads it by default and discards the malformed last command; if it is corrupted in the middle, Redis likewise discards just the bad command and keeps going. Running redis-check-aof with --fix is always safe, because it only removes the invalid command.

cases.answer: ANALYZE gathers the statistics the query planner relies on, and it can run on its own or as an optional step in VACUUM. Because ANALYZE samples rows randomly instead of reading every row, it is usually best to just analyze the whole database; by default it samples 30,000 rows per table. The autovacuum daemon schedules ANALYZE purely as a function of the number of rows inserted or updated, so it may skip a table whose statistical distribution changed meaningfully if only a few rows were touched. Changes to partitions or inheritance children do not trigger autoanalyze on the parent table, so an inheritance parent is never analyzed by autovacuum, and autovacuum runs ANALYZE on a partitioned table only after its partitions change significantly. A timestamp column that records each row's update time will probably need more frequent statistics updates than a column of URLs.

cases.answer: WAL write transactions write content once instead of twice, so they are faster than rollback-journal write transactions, and checkpoints are slower than WAL write transactions. It follows that a checkpoint is also slower than a rollback-journal write transaction. For read-heavy applications, WAL might be about 1% or 2% slower than rollback mode, and WAL performs worse than rollback mode for transactions over 100 MB in every SQLite version. Read performance in WAL mode deteriorates as the WAL file grows, so for maximum read performance one would checkpoint as often as every COMMIT. In the rollback-journal approach a COMMIT happens when the journal is deleted, whereas in WAL a COMMIT happens when a commit record is appended to the WAL, so a WAL commit never has to write to the original database file.
